newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Italy's ENI signs Libya gas deal - MEES.
newsitem.headline: Italy's ENI signs Libya gas deal - MEES.

text.p: Italian energy giant ENI has revealed in a recent share prospectus that it has signed a $3 billion gas supply deal with Libya, the Cyprus-based Middle East Economic Survey (MEES) newsletter reported on Monday.

The signature comes in the face of U.S. sanctions signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton which penalises non-U.S. firms from investing $40 million or more a year in the energy industries of Libya and Iran.

"Italy's ENI has now revealed for the first time that a $3bn gas production and supply deal with Libya -- known to have been under advanced negotiation for some time past -- was formally signed between it and Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) last June," MEES reported.

Agip, the exploration and production arm of Italy's energy giant ENI ENI.MIO has been negotiating with Libya for the export of eight billion cubic metres of Libyan natural gas a year by pipeline to Sicily.

The deal covers the export of gas from the Libyan onshore Wafa field and offshore Block NC-41 located off Libya's Mediterranean coast and a 520-km pipeline which would run between Libya and Capo Passero in Sicily.

MEES quoted the ENI prospectus that ENI and NOC "entered into an addendum to their 1974 exploration and production-sharing agreement for the joint development of the offshore natural gas and condensate fields in the NC-41 Block and the new onshore Wafa natural gas, oil and condensates field."
The tie-up would diversify Italy's dependenecy on gas imports from Algeria, Russia and Netherlands.
Three-quarters of the gas supplied would come from Block NC-41 and the remainder from Wafa, MEES reported.
In addition to Libya the company has also been eyeing supplies from Norway and the United Kingdom.
The size of the deal has been seen as a test case for U.S. sanctions penalising non-U.S. firms form investing $40 million or more a year in the energy industries of Libya or Iran.

EU officials have said that the deal could be hit by U.S. President Bill Clinton's Iran-Libya Sanctions Act which was signed in August to deter new investment to the two states which Washington sees as sponsors of international terrorism.
